scenes.spec: dipstick pulled and wiped, level below the hash marks; clean garage floor underneath
scenes.narration: Last episode, the driveway told the story. This time the driveway is spotless — and the dipstick keeps coming up low anyway. A quart gone every thousand miles, fifteen hundred, and no stain anywhere. That oil didn't leak. It went *through the engine* and out the tailpipe as smoke you mostly can't see. Burning oil is the leak with no puddle — and it runs on a completely different clock than the gasket stories. Some of it is normal. Some of it is a countdown. The difference is rate, color, and timing — all checkable from the driver's seat.

scenes.spec: channel card — "Why Is My Car Doing That?"
three-way split — "How fast? (quarts per 1,000 mi)" / "Blue smoke — when exactly?" / "Startup puff vs under load"
scenes.narration: **Rate first — and write it down.** Full mark, note the mileage, check every fuel stop. Manufacturers publish oil-consumption specs that surprise people — a quart in a thousand-plus miles is inside "normal" for plenty of modern engines, especially turbos. [TECH CONFIRM — the consumption threshold where YOU start caring: quarts per how many miles?] Below the threshold: monitor. Above: this episode. **Color: burning oil smokes BLUE-GRAY.** Not white (coolant steam, ep 4), not black (rich fuel). Blue is oil's signature — subtle, easiest seen in mirrors under hard acceleration or by the car behind you. **Timing is the diagnosis.** A puff at STARTUP that clears says one thing; smoke under ACCELERATION says another; smoke on DECELERATION — lifting off the gas downhill — says a third. Remember which one you have; the whole causes section is organized by it.

scenes.section: THE MECHANISM — HOW OIL GETS INTO THE FIRE
scenes.spec: cylinder closeup — piston with ring pack sealing against cylinder wall; above, valves sliding in guides with seals; oil mist everywhere outside the chamber
scenes.narration: The combustion chamber is supposed to be an oil-free zone, guarded at two borders. Below: the **piston rings** — springy bands around each piston that scrape the cylinder walls clean on every stroke. Above: the **valve stem seals** — little rubber caps where the valves slide down into the chamber. Oil mist fills everything *outside* those borders, lubricating constantly. Burning oil means a border is letting it through — and WHICH border is what the smoke-timing tells you.

scenes.section: CAUSE #1 — WORN VALVE STEM SEALS (the startup puff)
scenes.spec: engine parked overnight — oil seeping down valve stems past hardened seals, pooling on valve heads; morning start burns it: blue puff, then clear
scenes.narration: Park overnight and gravity goes to work: oil seeps past hardened valve seals, pooling on top of the closed valves. First start of the morning burns that pool off — a **blue puff at startup that clears in seconds**. That's the valve-seal signature: dramatic-looking, slow-moving, and the most benign entry in this episode. Consumption stays modest; many cars puff for years. [TECH CONFIRM — agree startup-puff cars can often run long-term, or do you counsel repair sooner?]

scenes.section: CAUSE #2 — WORN OR STUCK PISTON RINGS (the real consumption)
scenes.spec: ring pack — worn rings with poor wall contact; oil passing upward on intake stroke; blue smoke under load
scenes.narration: The rings are the big border, and when they wear — or gum up and stick in their grooves, a famous issue on some direct-injection engines [TECH CONFIRM — want to name engine families FHT sees for oil consumption, or keep it brand-neutral?] — oil rides up the cylinder walls into the burn. Signature: **blue smoke under acceleration** and consumption that climbs with every oil change interval. Confirmation is a **compression test or leak-down test** — the cylinders tell on themselves. This is the structural version of burning oil: it doesn't heal, it trends. [TECH CONFIRM — leak-down vs compression: your preferred confirm for ring wear?]

scenes.section: CAUSE #3 — PCV SYSTEM FAILURE (the impostor with a cheap fix)
scenes.spec: PCV path — crankcase vapors routed through valve back to intake; stuck valve pulling raw oil mist into the intake tract
scenes.narration: Before condemning rings, check the impostor. The **PCV system** recycles crankcase vapors back into the intake — through a valve that's supposed to meter the flow. When it sticks open, the intake vacuums raw oil mist straight into the chambers: sudden oil consumption, blue smoke, oily residue in the intake tract — on an engine whose rings are fine. The part is often absurdly cheap. Any sudden-onset oil burning: PCV first, always, before anyone says the word "rebuild." [TECH CONFIRM — a PCV save story would land great here; also typical PCV part/labor at FHT]

scenes.section: CAUSE #4 — TURBO SHAFT SEALS (for the boosted crowd)
scenes.spec: turbocharger — shaft between exhaust and intake wheels, oil-fed bearing in the middle, seals leaking into both housings
scenes.narration: Turbos spin on a shaft lubricated by engine oil at both ends, sealed from the air path. Worn turbo seals leak oil INTO the intake or exhaust stream: blue smoke (often on deceleration or right after), oil pooling in the intercooler piping, and a whistle that's changed character. On turbo cars this sits high on the suspect list — and it's a turbo job, not an engine job, which matters for the bill. [TECH CONFIRM — how much turbo work does FHT see? Keep/trim this section accordingly]

scenes.section: CAUSE #5 — JUST DRIVING IT LOW (the self-inflicted accelerant)
scenes.spec: feedback loop — low oil → hotter, dirtier remaining oil → faster wear → burns more → lower
scenes.narration: The quiet one: an engine run chronically a quart-plus low concentrates heat and contaminants in the oil that remains, accelerating exactly the ring and seal wear that burns more oil. Consumption problems *compound* if you don't keep the level up while deciding what to do. Checking and topping up isn't ignoring the problem — it's buying time at four dollars a quart. [TECH CONFIRM — bless this framing]

scenes.section: THE REPAIR — WHAT THE MONEY LOOKS LIKE
scenes.spec: decision tree — smoke timing in, jobs out
scenes.narration: Cheapest to dearest: **PCV valve** (parts money). **Valve stem seals** (mid; on many engines doable without pulling the head). **Turbo replacement/rebuild** (mid-to-large, but contained). **Piston rings** (engine-open territory — on high-mileage cars this triggers the same repair-vs-replace conversation as the cracked head in ep 4). And the modern middle path worth naming: some consumption cases respond to **piston-cleaning treatments/oil system flushes** targeted at stuck rings [TECH CONFIRM — does FHT use/endorse any de-coking or flush approach, or is that snake-oil-adjacent in your book? Honest answer either way is the beat]. [callout: typical US shop ranges — "PCV: $___–$___ · Valve seals: $___–$___ · Turbo: $___–$___ · Compression/leak-down test: $___–$___"] [TECH CONFIRM — fill from real FHT invoices]

scenes.spec: three-tier verdict card — "Monitor + top up" / "Diagnose this month" / "Engine off"
scenes.narration: **Monitor + top up:** consumption below the caring threshold, startup puff only, level held between checks. Keep a quart in the trunk and a log on your phone. **Diagnose this month:** consumption trending worse across intervals, smoke under load, sudden-onset burning (PCV check!), or a turbo tell. Trends don't reverse themselves. **Engine off:** oil light, knocking, or consumption so fast you're adding quarts weekly. That's not consumption anymore; that's an engine actively failing. [TECH CONFIRM — bless the tiers]

So: no puddle doesn't mean no problem — it means the oil is exiting through the fire. The rate says whether to care, the blue says it's oil, and the timing — startup, load, or lift-off — points at seals, rings, PCV, or turbo. Check the cheap impostor first, keep the level up while you decide, and let a compression test referee the big calls. That's both oil stories — the leak and the burn. Next time, the transmission gets its turn: slipping, and the difference between a fluid problem and a four-figure problem.
